bodies.thread:
Anthropic agreed to pay "at least" a staggering $1.5 billion, plus interest, to settle a class-action lawsuit regarding AI training.

The settlement payouts are expected to be "approximately $3,000 per book or work" involved in the case.

This figure is notable because the maximum potential penalty for the unauthorized use of books was "$150,000 per book" in this instance.

Under current United States legal interpretations, buying a physical book, scanning it, and training an AI on the digital output may qualify as fair use.

Anthropic stated that the specific digital copies involved in this settlement were not utilized to train its commercial AI models.

Technical challenges persist in AI, as "the correct way to model data entities depends entirely on the specific questions a user intends to answer."

The evolving legal landscape and complex data modeling requirements show that the path for AI development remains unsettled.

claims.text: Anthropic agreed to pay at least 1.5 billion dollars plus interest to resolve a class-action lawsuit brought by authors.
claims.verbatim: at least” a staggering $1.5 billion, plus interest

claims.text: The settlement payouts are anticipated to be roughly 3,000 dollars for every individual work.
The maximum potential penalty for the unauthorized use of books in this case was 150,000 dollars per title.
Under current United States legal interpretations, purchasing a physical book, scanning it, and training an AI on the digital output may qualify as fair use.
Anthropic stated that the specific digital copies involved in the settlement were not utilized to train its commercial AI models.
The correct way to model data entities depends entirely on the specific questions a user intends to answer.
Moonshot AI's Kimi-K2-Instruct-0905 model features a mixture-of-experts architecture with 1 trillion parameters.
claims.verbatim: 1 trillion parameters in a mixture-of-experts configuration

claims.text: Using LLM-generated summaries to embed images can significantly improve search recall compared to using standard CLIP embeddings.

hook_candidates: A 1.5 billion dollar settlement for AI training might actually be a discount for the company involved.
Scanning used books to train AI models is currently considered fair use in the United States.
Data modeling is often impossible because the right structure depends on the questions you have not asked yet.
Using LLM summaries instead of CLIP embeddings can boost image search recall from 28% to 75%.
The legal definition of a university is so complex that even identifying the name of Cambridge is a challenge.
voice_samples: It's wild to me that a $1.5 billion settlement can feel like a win for Anthropic, but given that it's undisputed that they downloaded pirated books (as did Meta and likely many other research teams) the maximum allowed penalty was $150,000 per book, so $3,000 per book is actually a significant discount.

To be clear: it appears it is legal, at least in the USA, to buy a used copy of a physical book (used = the author gets nothing), chop the spine off, scan the pages, discard the paper copy and then train on the scanned content.
I spent a long time building identifiers for universities and companies (which was taken for ROR later) and it was a nightmare to say what a university even was.

I am once again shocked at how much better image retrieval performance you can get if you embed highly opinionated summaries of an image, a summary that came out of a visual language model, than using CLIP embeddings themselves.
inventory.thesis: The legal landscape regarding AI training on copyrighted works is evolving through settlements and court interpretations of fair use, while technical challenges in data modeling and AI performance metrics remain complex.
